note: Which books each tradition receives as Scripture. Berean labels; it does not adjudicate. Every book listed here that Berean hosts can be opened and read in full — the point is to let you see the difference for yourself rather than take anyone's word for it.
honesty: The counts below are the ones each tradition commonly gives for itself, but no enumeration is fixed. Orthodox jurisdictions differ from one another; the Ethiopian "81" is counted several different ways by different lists; and 'canonical' has meant different things at different times — a book could be read publicly in worship without being used to settle doctrine. Where a tradition is genuinely divided, this file says so rather than picking a side.
framing: Nothing was subtracted from a single original Bible. There was never one agreed list that was later shortened. Different communities carried different collections, and the councils that spoke to it were mostly ratifying what their churches already read. The one case that does look like removal is narrow and real: the 1611 King James Bible included the Apocrypha, and British printers began leaving it out around 1826, largely a decision of Bible societies about cost and doctrine.

statusLabels.apocrypha: printed and read, but not used to establish doctrine
statusLabels.appendix: printed in an appendix, outside the canon

traditions.name: Jewish (Tanakh)
traditions.note: The same books as the Protestant Old Testament, counted and ordered differently: 24 rather than 39, because the Twelve Prophets are one book, as are Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra–Nehemiah.
traditions.shape: Torah · Nevi'im · Ketuvim — and it ends with Chronicles, not Malachi.

traditions.name: Protestant
traditions.note: 39 Old Testament, 27 New Testament. The deuterocanonical books were printed between the Testaments in Luther's Bible and in the 1611 King James, labeled Apocrypha — valuable to read, not used to establish doctrine.

traditions.name: Catholic
traditions.note: The 66 plus seven deuterocanonical books and the Greek additions to Esther and Daniel, affirmed at the Council of Trent in 1546. Three further books — 1 Esdras, 2 Esdras, and the Prayer of Manasseh — were printed in an appendix to the Vulgate, outside the canon.
traditions.shape: Old Testament (with the deuterocanon interleaved) · New Testament

traditions.name: Eastern Orthodox
traditions.note: The deuterocanon, plus books carried in the Greek Septuagint tradition: 1 Esdras, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151, and 3 Maccabees. 4 Maccabees is printed in an appendix. Slavonic and Russian usage differs from Greek — 2 Esdras is received there and not in the Greek churches.

traditions.name: Ethiopian Tewahedo
traditions.note: The widest canon of any ancient church, and the only one that receives 1 Enoch and Jubilees as Scripture. Its Meqabyan are three distinct Ethiopian books, not translations of the Greek Maccabees — a common confusion. The 'narrower' and 'broader' canons are both counted as 81 by different reckonings.
traditions.shape: Narrower and broader canons, both counted as 81

shared.note: All three Christian traditions receive the same 66 books; every disagreement below is about what to add to them, never about removing any of them. The 27-book New Testament is identical across all three.

books.name: Tobit
books.note: A family story of exile, marriage, and an angel travelling in disguise.

books.name: Judith
books.note: A widow saves her city by killing the general besieging it.

books.name: Esther (Greek)
books.note: Esther with six additions found in the Greek but not the Hebrew — including the prayers, which is where God is named at all.

books.name: Wisdom of Solomon
books.note: Greek-influenced wisdom writing; its portrait of the suffering righteous man is echoed in the Passion narratives.

books.name: Sirach
books.note: Also called Ecclesiasticus. A teacher's manual of practical wisdom; the Hebrew original was rediscovered in the Cairo Genizah and at Masada.

books.name: Baruch
books.note: Attributed to Jeremiah's scribe. Chapter 6 is the Letter of Jeremiah, counted as a separate book in Orthodox Bibles.

books.name: 1 Maccabees
books.note: The Maccabean revolt as history — the events behind Hanukkah, and the setting John 10:22 assumes.

books.name: 2 Maccabees
books.note: The same revolt told theologically. Chapter 7 is the earliest clear statement of bodily resurrection in Jewish literature.

books.name: Daniel (Greek)
books.note: Daniel with three additions: the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three inside chapter 3, then Susanna and Bel and the Dragon as chapters 13–14.

books.name: 1 Esdras
books.note: A Greek retelling of the return from exile, overlapping Ezra–Nehemiah and Chronicles.

books.name: Prayer of Manasseh
books.note: The repentance of the worst king in Judah's memory, fifteen verses long.

books.name: Psalm 151
books.note: David's own account of the shepherd boy and Goliath. A Hebrew version turned up among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

books.name: 3 Maccabees
books.note: Despite the name, not about the revolt — a rescue of Egyptian Jews under Ptolemy IV.

books.name: 4 Maccabees
books.note: A philosophical essay on reason mastering the passions, built on the martyrdoms of 2 Maccabees 7.

books.name: 2 Esdras
books.note: Also called 4 Ezra. Seven visions wrestling with why God let Jerusalem fall. Received in the Slavonic tradition, not the Greek.

books.name: 1 Enoch
books.note: The Watchers, the fallen angels, and the Son of Man. Quoted by name in Jude 14–15 — the New Testament cites a book almost no tradition kept.

books.name: Jubilees
books.note: Genesis and Exodus retold on a calendar of jubilees, with an accuser at the binding of Isaac and the Watchers of Genesis 6 named outright. Found in more than a dozen copies at Qumran — one of the most copied books there. Open it and read.

books.name: 1–3 Meqabyan
books.note: Three Ethiopian books, unrelated to the Greek Maccabees despite the name. Frequently confused with them in canon lists online.

books.name: 4 Baruch
books.note: Also called Paralipomena of Jeremiah — the fall of Jerusalem and Jeremiah's later days.

tanakhOrder.note: The same books as the Protestant Old Testament, in the Jewish order. The difference that matters most is the ending: a Christian Old Testament closes with Malachi promising a messenger yet to come, while the Tanakh closes with Chronicles and Cyrus saying “let him go up” — a call to return and rebuild. Same books, different final word.

sources: Council of Trent, Session IV (1546) — the Catholic canon defined, deuterocanon included.
Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Article VI (1571) — the Apocrypha read “for example of life and instruction of manners,” not to establish doctrine.
Westminster Confession of Faith I.3 (1646) — the Apocrypha given no authority in the church.
Synod of Jerusalem (1672) — the Orthodox response, receiving the wider Septuagint books.
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b — the order and contents of the Tanakh.
Codex Sinaiticus (4th c.) — the oldest complete New Testament, which also contains the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas.
